description: State, storage, API calls, caching, and offline on mobile.

screens.body:
Mobile data comes in three flavors. Ephemeral UI state lives in memory: which tab is open, what's typed in a field. Persisted local data survives restarts: settings, drafts, cached content. Server data is the source of truth that lives in your API.

Most bugs come from mixing these up — treating server data like it's instant, or storing a draft only in memory and losing it when the OS kills the app.

options: Their order history on the server
check.question: Which of these is ephemeral UI state?

screens.heading: Three kinds of mobile data
screens.keyPoint: Memory state, local persistence, and server truth are different jobs.

screens.body:
For small stuff — settings, flags, 'has seen onboarding' — key-value storage is perfect. React Native has AsyncStorage; native platforms have SharedPreferences and UserDefaults.

It's simple and fast, but it's not a database: don't stuff big lists in there, and never store secrets in it. It's readable by anyone with device access.

options: Simple key-value storage for small settings
check.question: Key-value storage is right for…

screens.heading: Simple local storage
screens.keyPoint: Key-value storage: great for flags and settings, not secrets.

screens.body:
Auth tokens, API keys, and anything sensitive belong in the platform's secure storage: Keychain on iOS, Keystore on Android. These are hardware-backed vaults the OS guards.

Plain key-value storage or a text file is not a vault. If someone gets the device, plain storage gives up your tokens with zero resistance. Rule of thumb: if losing it would hurt, it goes in secure storage.

options: A text file in app storage
check.question: Where should an auth token live?

screens.heading: Secure storage for secrets
screens.keyPoint: Tokens go in the OS vault, never in plain storage.

screens.body:
Every API call is async, slow, and fallible — so every screen that loads remote data needs three states: loading, error, and empty. Not just the happy path.

Use async/await with try/catch, set a timeout so a hung request can't freeze the screen forever, and always let the user retry. A failed request with a retry button beats a dead screen.

check.question: A screen loading remote data needs…

screens.heading: Calling APIs
screens.keyPoint: Async, slow, fallible — design for all three states.

screens.body:
Caching means keeping a copy of server data on the phone so the app opens fast and works offline. Show the cached copy instantly, then refresh quietly in the background — 'stale while revalidate.'

Give cached data an expiry (a TTL — time to live). Forever-cached data goes stale silently; never-cached data means a spinner on every open. Tune the TTL per screen: prices need freshness, help articles don't.

options: Show cached data instantly, refresh in background
check.question: A good caching strategy is…

screens.heading: Caching for speed and offline

screens.body:
When the user edits offline and someone else edits the same thing online, you get a sync conflict. The simplest resolution is last-write-wins: the newest timestamp wins, the older change is lost.

That's fine for a 'like' button and terrible for a shared document. Match the strategy to the stakes: timestamps for low-stakes, explicit merge or user choice for high-stakes edits.
screens.heading: Sync and conflicts
screens.keyPoint: Match conflict strategy to how much the data matters.

screens.body:
As screens share data, state gets messy: two screens each holding their own copy of the cart, disagreeing with each other. The fix is a single source of truth — one place that owns each piece of data, with screens reading from it.

Lift shared state up to a store or context both screens can read. When state lives in exactly one place, the whole app agrees.

options: One place owns each piece of data
Every screen keeps its own copy
check.question: Single source of truth means…

screens.heading: Keeping state sane
screens.keyPoint: One owner per piece of data — no competing copies.
